title: Load balancers deep
scopeHtml: Scope: L4 vs L7, balancing algorithms, sticky sessions, health checks, connection draining, LB high availability, global LB and anycast, with a sizing example. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why a load balancer and what it does
notes.html:
A load balancer (LB) is the single front door that spreads traffic over many servers, hides failures, and lets you change servers without clients noticing. It gives you: capacity (add servers), availability (skip dead ones), and flexibility (deploy gradually, route by path).

Worked example. Peak traffic 12,000 requests/s, one app server handles 1,500/s at 60% target CPU. You need 12,000 / 1,500 = 8 servers, plus one spare per AZ for failure: with 3 AZs run 12 servers (4 per AZ), so losing a whole AZ leaves 8, enough. The LB hides which of 12 answered.

Industry examples. AWS ALB/NLB, GCP Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Front Door, NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy; hardware F5. Google's Maglev and Meta's Katran are software L4 LBs on commodity servers.

Everyday analogy. The head waiter at a restaurant who seats guests at open tables, stops using a table with a broken chair, and lets you add new tables without telling the guests.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing a single LB box with no mention of its own redundancy.
  • No capacity maths for the pool or for N+1 / AZ loss.
  • Treating the LB as free: it has throughput, connection and TLS limits.

notes.title: L4 vs L7 load balancing
notes.html:
An L4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections; an L7 balancer understands HTTP.

  • L4: sees IP, port. Picks a backend at connection start and forwards packets (NAT or direct server return). Very fast (millions of packets/s per box), low latency (microseconds), protocol-agnostic (databases, MQTT, gRPC as raw TCP). Cannot look at URLs, cookies, or retry on 5xx.
  • L7: terminates the client connection, parses requests, can route by host/path/header/cookie, do TLS termination, rewrite, rate-limit, retry, canary by weight, add auth, and balance each request (not each connection). Costs more CPU (maybe 10x fewer requests/s per box) and adds about 0.1 to 1 ms.
L4 (NLB, Maglev, LVS) L7 (ALB, Nginx, Envoy)
Unit balanced connection request
Sees IP/port URL, headers, cookies
TLS passthrough or terminate terminate usually
Speed very high lower
Extras static IP, preserves source IP routing, retries, WAF, gRPC-aware

Decision gravity. Most apps want L7 (routing, observability). L4 in front of an L7 fleet is the large-scale pattern: L4 gives stable IPs and absorbs floods, L7 does the smart work. Switching later is mostly a DNS/endpoint change, so it is reversible, but clients with hard-coded IPs or allow-lists make the L4 static IP a sticky commitment.

Industry examples. Google's front end: Maglev (L4) then GFE (L7). Facebook: Katran (L4, XDP/eBPF) then Proxygen/Envoy-style L7. Cloudflare and AWS use the same layered idea. gRPC needs L7 (or client-side balancing) because one long HTTP/2 connection otherwise pins to one backend.

Everyday analogy. L4 is a postal sorting machine reading only the postcode; L7 is a clerk who opens the letter and routes by what it says.

Common interview traps.

  • Using L4 with gRPC/HTTP2 and getting one hot backend.
  • Forgetting the client's real IP is hidden behind L7 (use X-Forwarded-For or Proxy Protocol).
  • Saying L7 is always better; L4 is simpler and faster for non-HTTP.

notes.title: Load balancing algorithms
notes.html:
The algorithm decides which backend gets the next request. Pick based on request cost variation, connection length and whether you need affinity.

  • Round robin / weighted round robin: rotate; weights for unequal machines. Good when requests are similar and short.
  • Least connections / least outstanding requests: send to the backend with the fewest active ones. Better when request time varies a lot or connections are long (WebSockets, uploads).
  • Power of two choices (P2C): pick 2 random backends, send to the less loaded. Almost as good as full least-loaded with no global state; used by Envoy, NGINX (random two), Twitter Finagle. Avoids the herd problem where everyone picks the same "least loaded" server between load updates.
  • IP hash / consistent hashing: same key (client IP, user ID, URL) to the same backend; adding/removing a backend moves only about 1/N of keys. Good for caches (CDN, memcached proxies), sharded services. Bounded-load consistent hashing (Google paper, used in HAProxy, Vimeo) caps hotspots.
  • Random: simple, surprisingly good at scale.
  • Latency-aware / peak EWMA: weight by recent response time; slow nodes get less.

Worked example. 2 servers, 1,000 requests; 10% of requests take 2 s and others 20 ms. Round robin can by chance stack slow requests on one server (queue grows, p99 explodes) while the other idles. Least outstanding requests keeps both queues near equal. With 100 LB nodes each tracking only local counts, P2C still keeps the max queue length near log log N instead of log N.

Config example (nginx).

# upstream pool: least_conn with weights and failure handling
# upstream api {
#   least_conn;
#   server 10.0.1.10:8080 weight=3 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
#   server 10.0.1.11:8080 weight=1 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
#   keepalive 64;
# }

Industry examples. Envoy defaults to round robin and offers least request (P2C), ring hash, Maglev hash. AWS ALB offers round robin and least outstanding requests. Memcached/Redis clients and CDNs use consistent hashing.

Decision gravity. Algorithm is a reversible config. Consistent hashing becomes semi-sticky: data placement may depend on it (local caches warm), so changing it causes a cold cache stampede.

Everyday analogy. Supermarket checkouts: round robin is "next in line goes to lane 1, 2, 3..." even if lane 2 has a full trolley; least connections is "join the shortest queue".

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending round robin for long-lived connections.
  • Hashing on IP behind a NAT: thousands of users share one IP and hit one backend.
  • Not knowing consistent hashing's remapping property.

notes.title: Sticky sessions and session affinity
notes.html:
Stickiness sends the same client to the same backend. Methods: cookie set by the LB (AWSALB), source-IP hash, or a header/user-ID hash.

Why people use it: legacy apps with in-memory sessions, local caches that warm per user, WebSocket reconnect to the same node. Why to avoid it: it breaks even load (a heavy user pins a node), the session dies with the server, and rolling deploys lose sessions. Better: stateless servers with a shared store (Redis) or signed tokens. Use stickiness only as an optimisation where state is rebuildable.

Worked example. 10,000 users, 10 servers. Without stickiness each server has about 1,000 users. A power user group (a corporate NAT of 2,000 users) with IP-hash lands entirely on one server: 3,000 users there versus 800 elsewhere, 3.75x the load.

Industry examples. Early shopping carts in Java servlet containers used sticky sessions with Tomcat replication; modern shops use Redis or JWT. Gaming and chat edge servers use sticky routing by room or user ID (consistent hashing) deliberately.

Decision gravity. Starting sticky is easy; removing it later needs a state-externalisation project. If you must be sticky, design it as a hint, not as a requirement for correctness.

Everyday analogy. Always seeing the same doctor: nice continuity, but if she is on leave or overbooked, you wait or lose your notes unless they are in the shared file.

Common interview traps.

  • Using IP hash behind a corporate NAT or mobile carrier NAT.
  • Forgetting that a sticky node failure loses in-memory state.
  • Combining stickiness with autoscaling scale-in that kills the pinned node.

notes.title: Health checks
notes.html:
Health checks let the LB find dead or sick backends and stop sending them traffic. Two kinds:

  • Active: LB probes GET /health every N seconds. Parameters: interval, timeout, unhealthy threshold, healthy threshold.
  • Passive (outlier detection): LB watches real traffic; after e.g. 5 consecutive 5xx or connection resets, eject the node for 30 s (Envoy outlier detection, nginx max_fails).

Typical values: interval 10 s, timeout 3 s, unhealthy after 3 failures (30 s to detect), healthy after 2 successes. Faster interval means faster detection but more probe load and more flapping.

What should /health check? Shallow (process is up, returns 200) vs deep (checks DB, cache). Danger of deep checks: if the shared database hiccups, every server fails its check, the LB removes all of them, and a minor blip becomes a total outage. Common compromise: liveness (is the process alive) and readiness (can it serve now) kept separate, deep dependency checks only affect readiness of that instance for its own local problems, with the LB configured with fail-open / panic mode (Envoy: if more than 50% hosts are unhealthy, ignore health status and send to all).

# Kubernetes probes, typical values
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /live, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 6
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /live, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 2

Production incident pattern. A slow dependency makes the health endpoint time out; all nodes marked unhealthy together; 503s everywhere although nodes could serve cached data. Metric: healthy host count dropping to 0 while CPU is low. Another: restart loop from an overly strict liveness probe on a slow-starting JVM (needs a startup probe).

Industry examples. AWS ALB target group health checks, GCP, Envoy outlier detection and panic threshold, Kubernetes readiness gating of Service endpoints.

Everyday analogy. A shop manager who checks every few minutes that each till works, but does not close the whole shop because the card network is briefly slow.

Common interview traps.

  • Deep health checks that cascade a dependency failure to all nodes.
  • Using liveness probes that kill pods under load, making overload worse.
  • Forgetting warm-up: sending full traffic to a freshly started cold JVM (use slow start, slow_start / ALB slow start mode).

notes.title: Connection draining and graceful deploys
notes.html:
Draining (deregistration delay) means a backend that is leaving stops getting new requests but is allowed to finish the ones in flight. Without it, a deploy or scale-in cuts requests in half: clients see 502/connection reset.

Correct shutdown sequence:

  1. Mark the instance as draining (LB stops new requests). In Kubernetes: pod removed from endpoints.
  2. Wait for in-flight requests to finish, up to a timeout (ALB deregistration delay default 300 s; set to the max request time plus margin, e.g. 30 s for APIs).
  3. App receives SIGTERM, stops accepting, finishes work, closes idle connections, exits.
  4. If still running after the grace period, SIGKILL.

A classic gotcha in Kubernetes: the endpoint removal and SIGTERM race. Some LBs and kube-proxy keep sending traffic for a few seconds after SIGTERM, so add a preStop sleep of 5 to 15 s before shutting down.

# Kubernetes graceful shutdown
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
  - name: api
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }   # let LB/endpoints catch up

Worked example. Rolling deploy of 20 pods, each handles 200 requests/s with a p99 of 400 ms and 2% of requests being 20 s uploads. A drain of 30 s completes nearly everything; a drain of 0 s drops about 80 requests per pod instantly (in flight) = 1,600 errors across the deploy, visible as a spike in 5xx every release.

Industry examples. AWS ELB connection draining, Envoy drain_time, NGINX graceful reload (nginx -s reload keeps old workers until they finish), Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds, GKE and Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery. Long-lived connections (WebSocket) need a "go away" message (HTTP/2 GOAWAY) so clients reconnect elsewhere gradually.

Decision gravity. Setting this up is cheap and reversible; skipping it silently costs reliability on every deploy.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant announcing "last orders": no new guests, but those already seated finish their meal before the lights go off.

Common interview traps.

  • Deploys that cause a burst of 502s because of no drain or no preStop delay.
  • Drain timeout shorter than the longest request.
  • Reconnect storms when a draining server drops all WebSockets at once (spread with jitter).

notes.title: Making the load balancer itself highly available
notes.html:
The LB is a single point of failure unless you design it not to be. Patterns:

  1. Active-passive pair with a floating (virtual) IP: keepalived/VRRP; standby takes the IP in about 1 to 3 s on failure. Wastes half the capacity.
  2. Active-active behind DNS: several LB IPs in one DNS name (cloud LBs do this per AZ). Failover bounded by DNS TTL and client behaviour.
  3. Active-active with ECMP: the network router spreads flows over many L4 LB machines using equal-cost multi-path routing; LBs announce the VIP via BGP. Maglev and Katran use consistent hashing so that when an LB node fails, existing connections mostly keep the same backend.
  4. Managed cloud LB: AWS ALB/NLB scale automatically across AZs; you pay per LCU/GB.

Capacity notes: an L7 LB needs warm-up, and sudden 10x traffic can exceed what it has scaled to (AWS suggests pre-warming for planned spikes; ALB scales roughly with load over minutes). Limits to know: connections per node, TLS handshakes/s, bandwidth, ephemeral ports to backends (about 64k per backend IP:port, a cause of 502/connect failures at high rates without keepalive to backends).

Industry examples. Google Maglev (ECMP + consistent hashing, 10 Gbps+ per machine class), Meta Katran (XDP), GitHub's GLB director (consistent hash with a two-tier design), AWS NLB (static IPs per AZ).

Decision gravity. Self-managing LBs is an operations commitment; managed LBs are the default. Moving between them is a DNS cutover: reversible but needs care with TTL and allow-lists of IPs.

Everyday analogy. Instead of one receptionist at the door, have several at several doors, with a sign saying which doors are open.

Common interview traps.

  • Active-passive without testing failover.
  • Forgetting the LB's own connection/port limits.
  • Ignoring that DNS-based failover is slow.

notes.title: Global load balancing and anycast
notes.html:
Global load balancing sends users to the best region or data centre, not just the best server. Mechanisms:

  • DNS-based GSLB: return the IP of the nearest/healthy region (latency, geo, weighted, failover). Simple; limited by DNS TTL and resolver location.
  • Anycast: every region announces the same IP; BGP delivers users to the nearest. Quick failover when a site withdraws its route (seconds); used by CDNs and AWS Global Accelerator (2 static anycast IPs, traffic enters AWS network at the nearest edge and rides the private backbone to the region).
  • Global L7 front door: Google Cloud's single anycast VIP for all regions, Azure Front Door, Cloudflare. Terminates TLS at the edge close to the user (short handshake), then routes over a warm connection to the best healthy region.

What a global design must also solve: data locality (user data in region, replicate or route writes to a home region), failover capacity (if Region A dies, B must have headroom, typically run each region at 50 to 60% so the remaining can absorb), health at region level, and traffic shifting (drain a region gradually, 10% steps).

Worked example. Two regions, each 100k requests/s peak and 50k capacity headroom needed for failover: if each region runs at 50% of its max capacity (200k max), then on a regional failure the survivor must absorb 200k, exactly its limit. Active-active with N regions needs only 1/(N-1) extra headroom: with 3 regions you need each at 66% maximum utilisation to survive one loss.

Industry examples. Netflix evacuates a region by shifting traffic via DNS/Zuul ("regional evacuation" drills with Chaos Kong). Google uses one global VIP with Maglev + GFE. Cloudflare anycast across 300+ cities. AWS Route 53 latency + health checks and Global Accelerator.

Decision gravity. Going multi-region is a large one-way door for data: write routing, conflict resolution and cost double. Start with CDN + single region + a warm standby; add active-active only when SLA or latency demands.

Everyday analogy. A national airline's call centre: one number everywhere, routed to the nearest open office, with the other offices ready to take over if one closes.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "multi-region" without addressing data and write conflicts.
  • No spare capacity in the surviving region.
  • Relying only on DNS TTL for failover.

notes.title: Choosing and sizing: a worked design
notes.html:
Scenario. A food-ordering API: 20k requests/s peak, mix of REST (short) and a tracking WebSocket (long), users across India, mobile clients.

Decisions:

  1. Edge: CDN/anycast edge terminates TLS and speaks h2/h3 to phones (short handshakes), static content cached.
  2. Regional L7 LB (ALB/Envoy): path routing /api/*, /track/ws; least outstanding requests for API, least connections for WebSocket target group; 3 AZs; health check /ready interval 10 s, unhealthy 3, healthy 2; deregistration delay 30 s; slow start 30 s.
  3. Pool size: 20k / 1,500 per server = 14 at 100%; at 60% target CPU run 23, rounded to 24 (8 per AZ) so losing one AZ leaves 16 which handles 24k at 100% (acceptable for short failover with autoscaling).
  4. WebSockets: 500k concurrent connections at about 20 KB each = 10 GB of memory; spread over 12 tracking nodes; use "go away + jitter" on deploys.
  5. Observability: alert on target 5xx rate, healthy host count, p99 latency, LB 5xx versus target 5xx (distinguishes LB-generated 502/503/504 from app errors), active connections, rejected connections, surge queue length.

Production incident patterns.

  • LB 502 vs 504: 502 = bad response/connection reset by backend (often idle-timeout mismatch: LB idle 60 s, backend keep-alive 5 s closes first, so set backend keep-alive higher than LB idle timeout), 504 = backend too slow.
  • Retry storms: the LB or client retries a failing backend and doubles load; use retry budgets (Envoy: at most 20% extra) and jittered backoff.
  • Thundering herd after a restart: all caches cold, everything hits the DB. Use slow start and gradual ramp.

Everyday analogy. Planning a stadium: gates, queues, emergency exits and enough staff so that one closed gate doesn't stop the match.

Common interview traps.

  • No capacity maths or AZ-loss headroom.
  • Not distinguishing LB-generated errors from app errors in monitoring.
  • Idle timeout mismatches giving rare, hard-to-reproduce 502s.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An LB gives capacity, availability and flexibility; size the pool with maths (peak / per-server rate, target utilisation, N+1 per AZ).
  • L4 balances connections fast; L7 balances requests with routing and TLS. Large systems layer L4 in front of L7; gRPC needs L7 or client-side balancing.
  • Algorithms: round robin for uniform short requests, least outstanding requests for variable ones, P2C for distributed LBs, consistent hashing for caches and affinity.
  • Prefer stateless servers; sticky sessions are a fragile optimisation and break with NAT, deploys and failures.
  • Health checks: active and passive, tune interval/threshold, keep checks shallow to avoid cascading, separate liveness from readiness, use panic/fail-open mode, slow start for warm-up.
  • Draining plus preStop delay plus SIGTERM handling makes deploys error-free; match idle timeouts (backend > LB).
  • Make the LB itself redundant (VRRP, ECMP with consistent hashing, managed multi-AZ); global LB uses DNS GSLB or anycast with spare regional capacity and a plan for data locality.
